heroText: Accra is Ghana's capital and West Africa's laid-back beach-city gateway, mixing colonial-era forts with a fast-growing skyline along the Gulf of Guinea. First-time visitors should stand at Independence Square, wander the fishing lanes and murals of Jamestown, and pay respects at the Kwame Nkrumah Memorial Park. Kotoka International Airport puts Cape Coast's slave-fort history and Aburi's hills within easy day-trip range.

areas.name: Osu
areas.text: Osu is Accra's liveliest strip, packed with restaurants, bars and shops along Oxford Street, and a short walk from Labadi Beach.

areas.name: Airport Residential Area
areas.text: Airport Residential Area surrounds Kotoka International Airport with leafy streets, embassies and business hotels, convenient for short stays and early flights.

areas.name: East Legon
areas.text: East Legon is Accra's upscale suburb of malls, restaurants and gated homes, popular with longer-stay visitors wanting more space.

areas.name: Cantonments
areas.text: Cantonments is a quiet, embassy-lined district near Osu, offering calm streets with easy access to restaurants and the airport.

airports.name: Kotoka International Airport (ACC)
airports.text: Kotoka International Airport sits a few kilometres from central Accra; traffic can be heavy, so allow extra time for transfers at peak hours.

airportTransfer.value: Compare road transfer time between Kotoka International Airport (ACC) and central Accra before choosing an airport-area or city-centre hotel.

stayOverview: Base in Osu for nightlife, restaurants and beach access, or choose Airport Residential Area and Cantonments for embassies and easy airport transfers. East Legon suits longer stays needing malls, space and a quieter residential feel away from the coastal bustle.
hotelIntro: Accra hotel choice depends on purpose: Osu suits first-time visitors wanting restaurants and beach nightlife, Airport Residential Area and Cantonments suit business travelers near embassies and the airport, while East Legon offers newer hotels and malls for longer stays.
rentalCars: A rental car helps for day trips to Cape Coast or Aburi, but Accra's traffic makes ride-hailing apps the easier choice around the city.

travelTips.title: Best base
travelTips.text: Choose Osu or Airport Residential Area for an easy first stay near restaurants, embassies and quick airport transfers.

travelTips.title: Traffic
travelTips.text: Accra traffic is heavy at rush hour, so build extra time into airport transfers and cross-city trips, especially on the N1 highway.

travelTips.title: Cash and cards
travelTips.text: Carry Ghanaian cedi in small notes for markets and taxis, since card acceptance is inconsistent outside hotels and malls.

travelTips.title: Day trips
travelTips.text: Set aside a full day for Cape Coast's slave-fort history or a cooler half-day at the Aburi Botanical Gardens in the hills.

nearbyIdeas.name: Cape Coast
nearbyIdeas.label: Heritage
nearbyIdeas.text: Cape Coast Castle and Elmina Castle are UNESCO-listed slave forts about 2.5 hours west, essential stops for Ghana's Atlantic history.

nearbyIdeas.name: Aburi Botanical Gardens
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: The Aburi Botanical Gardens sit in cooler hills under an hour from Accra, good for a relaxed half-day away from the coast.

nearbyIdeas.name: Akosombo
nearbyIdeas.label: Nature
nearbyIdeas.text: Akosombo, home to the Volta River dam and Lake Volta, makes a good day trip for boat rides and hydroelectric history.

history.label: 15th century
history.text: By the late 15th century, the kingdom of Accra ruled the area from the capital at Ayawaso.
An early Portuguese fort was destroyed by the local inhabitants in 1576; trade afterwards was conducted on the beaches.

history.label: 17th century
history.text: The Dutch later built the nearby Fort Crèvecœur while the British and the Swedes built James Fort and Christiansborg castles, respectively, in the mid-17th century.
In 1873, after decades of tension between the British and Ashantis, the British captured Kumasi, destroying portions of the city.
The British then captured Accra in 1874, and in 1877, at the end of the second Anglo-Asante War, Accra replaced Cape Coast as the capital of the British Gold Coast.

As the newly established Gold Coast's administrative functions were moved to Accra (1877), an influx of British colonial administrators and European settlers grew around the Christiansborg (modern Osu, Ministries, Ridge, Labone, and Cantonments) began.
In 1918, the Grand Orange Lodge of Ghana was established in Accra to oversee and govern the local Ghanaian Orange Lodges.
For example, the segregation of European and African neighbourhoods was mandated by law until 1923, and all new buildings were required to be built out of stone or concrete.
In 1948, Ghana remained a colony of Great Britain following World War II.

However, the British Gold Coast ended before the Fry/Treavallion plan was enacted. Nkrumah Plan After Kwame Nkrumah became Ghana's first Prime Minister in 1957, he created his own plan for Accra's development.
